To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the carboxyic ionophores monesin and nigericn cause delays in the transport of influenza-virius envelope proteins through the Golgi complex and to the cell surface, and that they perturb the normal processing functions of this organelle.

the carboxyic ionophores monesin and nigeriin cause delays in both the processing and transport of newly synthesized influenza-virus envelope glycoproteins, haemaglutinin and neuraminidae, in Madin-Dary canine-kidney cell monolayers.

the ionophore monensin causes a block in oligo-saccharide-processing functions of the trans-Gol-gi complex and a slowing of the intracellular transport and plasma-membrane delivery of newly synthesized proteins in epithelial-cell monolayers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms involved in the intracellular processing, transport, and sorting of membrane and secretory proteins.
the mechanisms of intracellular transport and processing of viral and cellular membrane proteins in epithelial cell lines.
the mechanisms of protein sorting and intracellular transport in the secretory and endocytic pathways.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
monensin and/or nigericin are inhibitors of intracellular protein transport in MDCK cells.
the carboxyic ionophores monesn and nigericn inhibit the intracellular transport and processing of influenza virus envelope proteins in MDCK cells.
ionophores have an inhibitory effect on protein transport and processing in the Golgi complex and the endoplasmic reticulum.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ionophore treatment causes a slowing of intracellular transport and processing of the viral envelope proteins, and that the block in oligosacharide processing is in the trans-Golji compartment.

the ionophore monensin inhibits the processing and transport of viral envelope glycoproteins in Madin Darby canine kidney cells, and this inhibition is not due to a block in the formation of the trans Golgi network.

the ionophore monensin is an inhibitor of the intracellular transport and glycosylation of influenza virus haemagglutin and neuraminidases, but it has little effect on the intracellular transport or glycosylation of the influenza virus M2 protein.
The main takeaway from our work is that
monensin and other carboxylic acid ionophores are not specific inhibitors of Golgi function.
the carboxyic ionophore monensin is a potent inhibitor of influenza-virus replication in cultured cells.
the Golgi apparatus is a dynamic organelle, not static, as was once believed.
